sonnet.problem: The question repeats the verse's own phrase 'the rod of My anger', and the right answer ('The tool God uses to show His anger') just restates it, reusing 'anger'. The question effectively holds its own answer.
sonnet.rule: A choice card's question never holds its own answer, or a form of it, like "rock badgers" for "in the rocks." Ask something else.

sonnet.problem: The card tells a people destined for God's rage and being trampled, which is violence and judgment, yet it carries a joke ('one assignment you do NOT want to be on the other end of').
sonnet.rule: A card that tells death, violence, abuse, serious sin or the body's private matters has no joke.

sonnet.problem: The punchline has the same shape as card 1's joke ('you do NOT want your name right after it' versus 'one assignment you do NOT want to be on the other end of').
sonnet.rule: Each joke idea, comparison and punchline shape is used once per lesson.

sonnet.problem: Card 10 already puts 'Jerusalem and Samaria' side by side, and card 11's question repeats them. Card 12 then says Samaria is already done, so the blank can only be Jerusalem. Earlier cards give the answer away.
sonnet.rule: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

sonnet.problem: The choice card asks about what the king says in verse 13 before any story card has told it. Story card 4 then tells verse 13, quoting 'By the strength of my hand I have done this', which gives away the answer and makes the question a blind guess.
sonnet.rule: Cards follow the passage in order. A choice card can look back at a verse an earlier card in the same stop told, but never jumps ahead.

sonnet.problem: The right answer ('Nobody even tried to stop him') says what the bird-silence picture stands for. Verse 14 gives the picture but not its meaning.
sonnet.rule: He retells the picture as the text gives it and says what it stands for only when the passage says so.

sonnet.problem: The statement says that in the axe picture Assyria is the axe and the LORD is the one swinging it. Verse 15 only asks the question and does not say what the axe and the swinger stand for.
sonnet.rule: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect. This includes what a picture means.

sonnet.problem: A prediction is told in the present tense as if it is happening ('comes for Assyria's thorns and thistles', 'the splendor ... goes too'). Verses 16-18 say 'will'.
sonnet.rule: A prediction stays a prediction: "God says Tyre will fall," never "Tyre falls."
